patient_information: A 42-year-old British male expatriate who has lived in Malawi for 18 months.
chief_complaint: Florid itchy rash, difficulty in breathing, and a feeling he is going to die.
history_of_present_illness: Two days prior to admission, he believed he was bitten by a tick on his ankle while walking in the countryside; 24 hours later, he noticed a circumscribed, painless, indurated lesion on his left ankle, accompanied by fever and arthralgia, for which he was treated with paracetamol after a negative malaria blood film; on the day of admission, he developed a widespread itchy rash, progressive inability to breathe, and faintness; he has a family history of allergy, previously kept bees without ill effect, and 9 months prior experienced an asthmatic attack after insect bites at Lake Malawi.
exposure_and_epidemiology: Lived in Malawi for 18 months; suspected tick bite 2 days prior to admission; visited a national game park 2 weeks before current illness where he suffered numerous painful bites by tsetse flies.
vitals: Temperature 38°C, pulse rate 130 bpm, systolic blood pressure 60 mmHg.
physical_exam: Clammy, in a state of collapse, widespread urticarial rash, respiratory distress, stridor, an indurated circumscribed swelling on the inside of his left ankle, and expiratory wheezes on chest auscultation.
labs_and_diagnostics: Haemoglobin 17.4d/dL; white cell count 6.1 G/L (polymorphs 85%, lymphocytes 10%); erythrocyte sedimentation rate 5 mm/hour; blood film negative for malaria parasites; chest radiograph normal; stool and urine microscopy negative; thick blood film later revealed 5 to 10 trypanosomes per high power field; CSF normal 24 hours after first suramin dose; urine showed protein, casts, and white cells towards end of suramin treatment, which later disappeared.
differential_diagnosis: Possible hypersensitivity reaction to a tick bite, invasive helminthiasis (acute schistosomiasis, acute fascioliasis, Loeffler's syndrome), rickettsial disease, and connective tissue disease.
management_and_clinical_course: Initial management for anaphylactic shock with 0.5ml of 1:1000 adrenaline intramuscularly with good effect; admitted to hospital and treated for 2 days with intermittent intramuscular adrenaline, intravenous hydrocortisone, and oral antihistaminics for urticaria, stridor, and wheezing; on day 3, stridor and wheezing ceased, urticarial rash replaced by a diffuse erythematous rash, face became puffy, bad headache, and sustained fever of 38-39°C; subsequently diagnosed with trypanosomiasis and given a test dose of suramin 0.25 g, followed by 0.5 g 2 days later, 1.0 g another 2 days later, then weekly doses of 1.0 g to a total of 5.75g suramin.
final_diagnosis: Human African Trypanosomiasis (HAT), specifically East African trypanosomiasis (Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense), with anaphylactic shock.
